query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount (~0.2 at. % Y) of yttrium during the synthesis of a refractory high-entropy alloy improves its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy processed without reactive element additions that exhibits rapid oxidation and oxide scale spallation at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.2 at. % yttrium into the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure at approximately 1300 °C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., air) for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of yttrium to the oxide/alloy interface facilitates the formation of a dense and protective oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3) that adheres well to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The reactive element effect from yttrium reduces oxygen ion diffusivity and improves oxide adhesion by catalyzing a more uniform, slow-growing protective oxide layer, thereby mitigating rapid oxidation and scale spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain and fewer spallation events, leading to improved integrity of the oxide scale compared to the undoped, baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Refractory HEA without yttrium addition exposed under the same high-temperature, oxygen-rich conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under the specified conditions (1300 °C, air, 100-hour exposure) and for alloys with compositions and microstructures similar to those in the current design; deviations in composition or processing might influence effectiveness.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by the reactive element effect observed in other high-temperature alloys, the exact degree of improvement and scale microstructure details in this refractory HEA are uncertain and may vary with processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples with identical base compositions: one set with the addition of ~0.2 at. % yttrium and a control set without yttrium. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 1300 °C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, assess the oxidation behavior using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to measure weight gain and employ scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for oxide scale integrity and adhesion analysis.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and adherence via SEM and cross-sectional microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction (for example, at least 20% lower weight gain or improved scale adhesion) compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . frame.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) intended for structural applications, initially lacking enhanced high‐temperature oxidation resistance.
frame.goal: Improve the alloy’s resistance to oxygen attack at extreme temperatures by ensuring the formation of a stable, adherent protective oxide scale.
frame.limitation: Under extreme temperatures, the untreated alloy suffers from rapid oxygen attack leading to scale spallation and degradation of mechanical properties.
constraints: single intervention must be effective (no combination treatments)
suitable for bulk alloy processing rather than a surface-only treatment
must meet structural requirements under extreme-temperature conditions
frame.regime: High temperature (e.g., 1200–1400 °C) in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (such as air or pure O2) for extended exposure (e.g., 100 hours) simulating service conditions.
prior_attempts: Use of conventional pre-oxidation treatments or surface coatings, which have been impractical or insufficient for bulk refractory HEAs
Alloy formulations without reactive element additions have shown excessive oxidation and oxide scale spallation at high temperatures
frame.understanding: The hypothesis leverages the reactive element effect where trace additions (e.g., yttrium) promote the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer (likely Al2O3 or comparable scale), which acts as a barrier by lowering oxygen ion diffusivity and enhancing scale adhesion. Introducing a minor concentration of a reactive element during alloy synthesis is expected to suppress detrimental oxidation kinetics and reduce scale spallation compared to the untreated alloy.
frame.method: Add a low concentration (e.g., ~0.2 at. % Y) of yttrium during alloy synthesis. The hypothesis predicts that Y will segregate to the oxide/alloy interface during high-temperature exposure, catalyzing the formation of a dense, slow-growing protective oxide scale. Prior studies in Ni-based superalloys and other high-temperature alloys have shown that reactive element doping improves scale adherence and slow oxidation kinetics. The experiment would compare the oxidation weight gain and scale integrity between the Y-doped alloy and the undoped control after exposure at 1300 °C in air for 100 hours. A clear falsification criterion would be if the Y-doped sample shows no statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., weight gain or scale adhesion failure) relative to the untreated alloy.

cues_for: enhanced adhesion of the oxide scale
cues_against: alloy formulations without reactive elements have shown excessive oxidation
families.best_lever: Add a low concentration of yttrium during alloy synthesis to promote formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide layer such as Al2O3.

improvement in interfacial bonding between oxide and alloy

families.best_lever: Engineer the alloy’s in-situ interface characteristics during synthesis to promote reactive element segregation at the oxide/alloy boundary, although this is secondary to a direct compositional change.

families.principle: Heat treatments can control oxide layer formation and adherence by modifying diffusion rates and phase stability at high temperatures.

families.best_lever: Implement a controlled thermal treatment post-synthesis aimed at stabilizing a protective oxide scale, although prior evidence suggests limited effectiveness compared to compositional adjustments.
